Who does not know, or has not heard of
Rev. Jacob Young, the patriarch of Method-
ism in the United States? The good old
man died at the residence of his son in Harris-
burgh, Friday, at the advanced age of 83
years, and Sunday afternoon his funeral
sermon was preached in the Town street
church, by the venerable Joseph Carper,
of Somerset, a co-laborer of the deceased
to the cause of religion. The church was
filled to overflowing, hundreds being unable
to obtain seats, were obliged to stand in
the aisles, and entrance. The street was
blocked with carriages for half a square in
front of the church; indeed, it seemed as
if everybody wanted to pay their last tri-
bute to the man that had devoted a long
life to Christ and Him only. About half
past four, the funeral train was formed and
slowly, sadly wound its way to Green
Lawn Cemetery, where the body was en-
tombed. The procession was the largest
that has been on our street for years.

Jacob Young was born in what is now
called Allegheny county, Pennsylvania,
March 18th, 1776, and in September 1801
he was licensed to preach, and began in
Shelby county, Kentucky, as an itinerant,
and was placed on the Wayne (Ky.) Cir-
cuit in 1809. In 1805 he was appointed
on the Marietta Circuit; and in 1806 was
sent to Tennessee, from there to Mississ-
ippi; then to Virginia, and Maryland next.
In 1819 he came again to Ohio and re-
mained here until his death. He acted as
Presiding Elder to most of the districts of
the State, being on the Columbus district
from 1835 to 1849, and closed his itinerant
labors in 1856 on the Rehoboth Circuit,
because of exhaustion and failure of eye
sight. He was superannuated at the New
ark Conference in 1855 at the age of 80
years, having been in the ministry 80
years. Indeed it may be said in the minis-
try till his death, for he occasionally preach
ed at various places. He was present at
the Conference held here the first of this
month, and his counsels were of great
weight.

$19,409,882. During the first nine months of
1857, the import revenue derived by France
from it was over $25,000,000, four-6ths of
which were exported from the United States.

next to salt, is probably the article most con-
sumed by men. In one form or another, but
most generally in the form of fume or smoke,
there is no climate in which it is not consumed,
and no nationality that has not adopted it. To
put down its use has equally baffled Legislators
and moralists, and, in the words of Pope, on
higher subject, it may be said to be partaken
of "by saint, by savage, and by sage." The
average consumption per head of male popu-
lation over eighteen years of age, in some
countries, seems almost fabulous. In the Ger-
man States included in the operation of the
Zollverein and the Steuerverein, it reaches from

EXCITEMENT AT HOLLY SPRINGS.—We are
informed that a merchant of Boston obtained a
requisition from the Governor of Massachusetts,
on the Governor of Mississippi, for the body of
a merchant at Holly Springs, who was charged
with obtaining goods under false pretences
from the Boston merchant. The proper writ
was granted by the Governor of Mississippi to
an agent of the Boston merchant. Armed with
this writ, the agent proceeded to Holly Springs
last week, and made the arrest. On his arri-
val there, his business was soon found out,
public meeting called, and resolutions adopted,
to the effect that Massachusetts, having always
resisted the rendition of slaves, had no right of
any sort of requisition upon the people of
Mississippi, and that the agent of the Boston
house be notified to leave, or he would be
trotted through. Of course, he left, burned
all his "requisition papers," and promised
never to return.—Traveler, 29th ult.


The company of colored people, under the
lead of a barber named Draper, are to leave
Cleveland for Liberia immediately. They pro-
pose to go to farming in the interior of the coun-
try.


Some of the Opposition journals persist in
the assertion that the President was in favor of
calling an extra session, but was overruled by
the heads of the Departments. Nothing can be
more opposite to the truth than this statement.


DESTRUCTIVE FIRE IN ST. LOUIS.—St. Louis,
April 1.—The extensive variety store of Speck
& Co., Main street, was destroyed by fire
last night involving loss of $95,900, of which
$4,000 was covered by insurance. The adjoin-
ing store of Enders Co. was damaged to the
extent of $10,000—fully insured.


The Santa Fe mail of the 10th has reached
Independence. The store of Garland Co.,
which suffers at Fort Stanton, had been destroyed by
fire, loss $17,900. The transportation of the
California mail via the Pony Express has been
suspended in consequence of the interference
of Indians. It was understood that Lieut. Beale
had turned back, but the cause of his doing so
was unknown.


A large meeting of shoe dealers and manu-
facturers has been held at Boston, and, after
discussion, a committee of nine was appointed
to confer with the New York dealers, with
view of procuring more accurate inspection
of sole leather.

"All
right sir," he replied, and he stepped into
the cabin where sure enough the above
named couple stood waiting.

There had been some "kissing games"
and several mock marriages gone through
with during the evening, and supposed
this was merely a continuation of the
sport; and so thought the "preacher,"
who, I could see, had a good deal of hu-
mor in him, and was inclined to promote
general good feeling and merriment.--
The couple stood up before him, in a good
deal more solemn than was necessary in a
mock marriage, (I thought) and the
preacher asked the necessary ques-
tions, and then, proceeding in the usual
way, announced them "husband and
wife."

There was a good deal of fun after-
wards, and when it was over I left the
cabin--and so did the preacher who
remarked to me that he liked to see the
young folks enjoy themselves, and took a
good deal of pleasure in contributing to
their fun; but he did not understand why
they should select him to act as preach-
er.

Just then some one called me aside, and
the old gentleman stepped into the state-
room, which was next to mine. When I
returned the door stood open, and the
preacher stood just inside, with his
coat and vest off, and one boot in his hand,
talking with the gentleman who played the
"attendant," and who, as I came up, re-
marked:

"Well, if that is the case it is a good
joke; for they are in dead earnest, and
have retired to the same stateroom."

The old gentleman raised both hands as
he exclaimed, "GOOD Heavens! you don't
tell me so!" and rushing just as he was,
boot in hand, to the stateroom indicated,
commenced an assault on the door as if
he would batter it down, exclaiming at
each lick: "For Heavens sake don't I
am a preacher!"

The whole cabin was aroused, every
stateroom flying open, and the "Arkan-
sas traveller" poking out his head, cool-
ly remarked: "OLD Hoss YOU'RE TOO
LATE!"

EL PASO Nov. 9th 1859.

EDITOR ARIZONAS.—The green mantle of nature vanishes with each passing hour, and the sere and failing leaf warns us of the approach of winter. The last petals of the summer flowers have fallen, and their fragrance wafted far away, upon the desert air. The golden-winged butterfly, made sportive bathing in the nectar of roses, has returned to its silken cell to dream until Spring shall return again. The merry swallows, with their full-fledged broods, have quit their tiny abodes, beneath the projecting caves, and fled upon their swift pinions in search of more congenial climes. AURORA has doffed her brilliant robes and assumed one of dusky hue, resembling the dirty black gown of the song ennobled widow. It is now that "parting day dies like the dolphin, when each pang imbues with a new color." The sombre days of the Indian Summer bring reflection to the soul, and we admire the variety of the beauties of nature. The crimson leaf and brown meadow seem like old friends in adversity, and the heart still cherishes and clings to them. It is now, that many a heart bounds with joy in anticipation of "hog-killing season," and youths dream of cracking bread, and spare ribs. The bare-footed boy skips like the nimble fawn, at the idea of strutting in a pair of brand new boots, when winter comes, which brings its sweets as well as its bitters and which modern science demonstrates mixed up with a little whisky forms the cocktail, said by philosophers to be an excellent substitute for milk.

El Paso is rapidly improving, and bids fair in short time, to vie with the beautiful and flourishing town of Mesilla of your Territory. Through the wise counsels and indefatigable energy of our worthy Mayor and Aldermen the City is again supplied with water, thus, giving to the patrons of the Groceries opportunity to mix, if they see proper. All classes and professions seem to be driving fair business, and the autumn weather lends an air of activity to the place.

The happy and smiling faces of the Senoritas as they cast one eye on fellows from beneath their bonnets, seems to indicate that peace reigns in Warsaw, and they don't care a fig for the price of corn.

The Saloon of Messrs Cook & Cameron, of this place, was last night robbed of $500; there appears to be no suspicion as to who committed the burglary.

The grand feast which is to come off in El Paso de Mexico on the 5th of December, is looked forward to with much pleasure and the Col. now engaged in breaking in a pair of new boots for the bailes to come off on that interesting occasion.

The demand for Chihuahua dogs has diminished very much since the imposition upon Mexico of certain tax, upon our pup, purchased some months ago.

But it may be objected that we have no proof that medicines can act thus certainly on the lungs, or on the system through the lungs. To developing this portion of the subject shall devote my letter to-day. Inhalation of chlorine will produce a temporary arrest of the secretion of the bronchial tubes, or in other words, dryness of the surface. The use of expectorant and emollient vapors will produce the directly opposite effect, and in the first stage of acute bronchitis, when the tubes are dry and tumid no remedy by the stomach will produce the resolution of this state, with anything approaching the speed with which such inhalants act. If the patient sitting up at two in the morning choking in all the agonies of the worst fit of asthma, an anti-spasmodic inhalant will procure perfect relief for the night in three or four minutes. If the case be one of chronic bronchitis, where the secretion is profuse and semi-purulent, the use of balsamic and astringent inhalants will soon diminish the quantity and improve the quality of the expectoration. These are facts patent to the observation of every medical man, who will take the trouble to make the trial. But it will serve to make the power of inhaled remedies over the general system more evident; a few examples be given. The power of chlorine and iodine over consumption is proved by the exemption of workmen from this disease who work in factories where the vapors are floating about in the air, and by cures being effected upon the tuberculized by resorting to such establishments for work.

Priory gained his fame for curing consumption, by pouring in iodine in every way, by inhalation and otherwise. But he often left his patients, as Dr. Kingston said, the victim of iodism, scarcely less deplorable state than the victims of mercurialism. This unhappy result is avoided by combining the use of various vegetable discutients, that aid the effects of iodine, and procure salutary effects of their own. A drachm of chloroform will produce little or no effect when taken into the stomach, but the same quantity inhaled into the lungs will cause profound intoxication, with total loss of sense and motion, and even death. A grain of arsenuretted hydrogen swallowed has little effect, but the hundredth part of a grain inhaled into the lungs, will cause death, with all the symptoms of arsenical poisoning. The late professor of chemistry in Calcutta College, was exhibiting Marsh's test to his class, and an accidental draught blew the fumes toward him, and he inhaled perhaps not the thousandth of a grain, certainly not the five hundredth; he was seized with violent arsenical poisoning, and his life was imperiled for some time. Gen. Gates, who introduced the use of stramonium leaves when smoked, for the relief of asthma, fell victim to an overdose, and yet the quantity of empyreumatic oil introduced into the lungs must have been very minute. The preceding remarks have been thrown together, to prove that medicines inhaled into the lungs produce not only direct local effects, but are capable of acting in the system at large, as alteratives, narcotics, discutients, etc., and these in very much smaller doses than by the stomach. They are adduced as specimens of the proofs upon which the practitioners of inhalation rely for the maintenance of their assertions, and these proofs might be accumulated ad infinitum. With this preamble my readers will be able to understand the rationale of the process by which cure is effected through inhalation, which will form the subject of my next letter.

N. B. WOLFE, M. D.
Physician for diseases of the Lungs and Throat, No 50, Ninth street, Cincinnati, O.

FOURTH WARD INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL.—The ladies
connected with the Fourth Ward Industrial School are
soliciting the charity of the public for a new building.
They say:


"On the lot of January, 1859, although our pupils,
individually cost us but six per annum our treasury
was empty and a small debt had been contracted. To
drive them to their comfortless homes—in some cases to
drunken fathers, to mothers worse than drunkards—
the 100 little girls who assemble in our school
rooms was more than could be contemplated.
We have reasonable hope that, under our care, they
are training for the real world well; for if they
are deprived of that care, they must beg, lie, cheat,
perhaps sink lower—or starve. As we cannot ex-
pect the strength of martyrs in children of from 20
years of age, it is not doubtful whether they succeed.
As a general rule every child brought under our
care and protection is saved from being maintained, at
the public expense, in our prisons and penitentiaries.


Through appeals made by some of the ladies con-
nected with the School, to their personal friends,
money has been collected to meet our immediate
wants. But that is not enough—it is of importance
to the community that the Fourth Ward Industrial
School should become a permanent institution; we,
therefore, call upon the public to save us from de-
pending altogether upon anything so precarious as
individual subscriptions and donations.


We ask for $9,000 of $10,000, to enable us to pur-
chase a house and to make such arrangements as are
necessary to educate our pupils for their station in
life. We wish to teach them washing, house
cleaning, scullery work, baking, such plain cooking
as is done in this establishment, in addition to the use
of the needle and the sewing machine, and the common
branches of English education in which they are
presently instructed. With this training, the children,
instead of growing up as disgrace to their age and the
curse of society, will add to its comfort by doing
what we so much need—skillful and well-trained
matrons.


Donations may be sent to either of the officers of
the Society, to the Children's Aid Society, Clinton
Hall, Astor Place, or to Mr. John Earle Willis,
Metropolitan Bank, marked "Fourth Ward Industrial
School."

SENTENCE OF CANCEMI.


To be Imprisoned for Life—Statement of the Prisoner.


SUPREME COURT—GENERAL TERM.
Presiding, Judges Davies, Clark, Ingraham and Sutherland.


The District Attorney moved the judgment of the Court Michael Cancemi convicted at the Circuit for the manslaughter of Eugene Anderson. On making the motion, the plea in that should be filed.


Mr. Ashmead asked permission to read to the Court a document which he had prepared, in order to put himself and his colleague Mr. Brinkman right with the profession and the public.


District Attorney objected unless he first had opportunity of seeing the document.


The Court did not think it necessary for the counsel to vindicate themselves.


Mr. Ashmead said that he desired that what he had written might go on the record. Mr. Ashmead, then proceeding with his objections, the overriding of the plea at bar by the Circuit judge when he was again inter-rogated. Cancemi was then asked where he was born, to which he answered, in Sicily, and that he is a bookbinder by trade.


In answer to the question what he had to say why the sentence of the Court should not be pronounced against him, he made a statement which had been translated by Mr. Cristadoro and which he would now read. Mr. Ashmead, while reading the statement, moved to tears and Mr. Brinkman concluded the reading. The following is a copy:


In reply to the question why sentence should be pronounced upon me, I, Michael Cancemi, having been convicted and am most unjustly to suffer, I was years ago when I landed was poor and friendless, and came to the city of New York where I acquired knowledge of the trade. I have served the interests of my employers although constant trials and many accusations were made against me. They were my friends and they cheerfully testified to my character and my willingness to serve, and they were acquitted to receive me again into their confidence. I avail myself of this opportunity to plead against and for which I am about to suffer human punishment. I am a person of good character, to whom the surrounding circumstances were unknown. I was born in Sicily, and it was the habit when murders or assassins were present, for the witnesses to be taken into custody and for the person to be taken away. I was walking along Elm street when heavy footsteps attracted my attention and I felt alarm. I turned towards the door and by the collar I caught him. I spoke the truth and make it with the consciousness that I am a man of honor. On a distant day I shall render something to him, whom all say was Eugene Anderson. I was in some sense apparently innocent of the crime, and it was not taken by human hands in order that the full justice be expressed. I am grateful to the counsel who have made themselves sacrificing spirit, generously and ably conducted my defence. I can easily describe and I thank God. I am grateful for the kindness rendered to me by my accomplices, Mr. Joseph Cristadoro and other friends, to whom my situation was unknown until now. I ask for blessings Him who said I am in prison, and we visited him. I have been injured by unsound words and acts and who sought to prejudice the public against me and my cause. I am ready to receive whatever sentence the Court will pronounce, but it is human to ask that it may be tempered with mercy.


Judge Davies said that the sentence of the Court would be pronounced by the Judge before whom the prisoner was tried.


Judge Ingraham then pronounced the following sentence, which was interpreted to him by Mr. Kazinski:—Michael Cancemi charged with the manslaughter of Eugene Anderson, policeman while on duty on the 21st July 1861. He who caused the death of Anderson had previously been connected with burglary in the corner of Grand and Centre streets, and while endeavoring to arrest him, he caused the death. Such repeated convictions of you by three juries, faithful exertions assigned you, who have defended with much zeal, those verdicts aside, connected with the question of your guilt upon the last trial. The Jury, either from motives of pity or other cause not known to the Court, have found you guilty of manslaughter in the first degree. While not disposed to find fault with the verdict of the jury at this time, I think there is no doubt but that the evidence of the trial amply sufficient have sustained the charge against you of murder. The weapon which was used by you was a loaded weapon, used with the intent of taking the life of him who might interfere to prevent escape from the premises, and without preparation, you sent the victim of your crime into another world. We have been unable to find anything that would mitigate your guilt or justify the Court in imposing a heavier punishment. Had the jury found a similar verdict with justice, your punishment would have been death, and although your life has been spared, nothing you cannot be considered by the Court after the verdict of the jury. If they are entitled to any weight, they must be. You, Michael Cancemi, for which you have been convicted, be confined in the state prison for the duration of your natural life.


The prisoner, who heard the sentence with calmness, was then removed.

ARESSBURG, May 15, 1880.


Sir—I accept the rights of citizen of Thurgovia with the greatest pleasure. I am glad that new ties bind me to that country which, for sixteen years, has extended to me its most generous hospitality. My position as an exile renders me doubly sensible to the interest you show me. As a Freedman and a Bonaparte I am proud of being citizen of a free country.


In 1831 he published work on Artillery, for the use of the Swiss troops. For this he was made Captain of Artillery. In his acknowledgements he says:


I am proud of being numbered among the defenders of a state in which the sovereignty of the people is considered as the basis of the Constitution, and where every citizen is ready to sacrifice himself for the liberty and independence of his country.

ARESSBURG, Jan. 30, 1888.


As to my position, believe me, I understand it fully, although it is very complicated. I feel that as yet, I am only known by name, not by my deeds. I am an aristocrat by birth, a Democrat by nature and by opinion. I owe all to inheritance and acquire everything from elan. Courted by some for my name, by others for my title—taxed with personal ambition as soon as I step beyond my accustomed sphere, accused of apathy and indifference, I remain galant—in short inspiring both liberals and autocrats with fear because of the influence of my name. I have no political friends but among those who, accustomed to the caprices of fortune, think that, by some chance, I may one day be useful. It is because I see all the difficulties that would impede my progress in the gaining of any career that I have made it a rule to follow the impulses of my heart, my reason and my conscience, and never to regard any consideration of secondary importance when I believe that I am acting for the general interest in short, to walk in a straight line without needing all the difficulties that obstruct my path.


He was twenty seven years of age when those lines (the language of almost prophecy) were penned. THE ENCYCLICAL LETTER OF THE POPE


To our venerable Brethren the Patriarchs, Primates, Archbishops, Bishops, and other priests in communion with the Holy See, Pius IX, Pope. Venerable Brethren, apostolic health and benediction:—


In celebrating with the effusion of joy, in these holy days and in the whole world the solemn anniversary of the pascal mystery, our holy mother the Church exults in the memory of all the faithful the consoling words of that happy peace which the only Son of God, Our Lord Christ resurrected, after having conquered death and destroyed the tyranny of the devil has so often and with so much love announced to his disciples; and now at the same time the sinister cry of war among the Catholic nations and resounds to all.


Holding on earth, notwithstanding our unworthiness, in the place of Him who, coming from the bosom of the Father, brought peace to men of good will who, rising from the dead and ascending to heaven to sit at the right of the Father left peace to his disciples; and induced by particular and heartfelt sentiments of our love and solicitude principally towards the Catholic nations we cannot refrain from always preaching peace and applying ourselves with all the strength of mind to inculcate to all the very words of divine Saviour often repeated: Pax! Pax! It is with those words of peace that we lovingly address you venerable brethren who are called to solicitude, so that in your piety you should excite by your zeal and efforts the faithful entrusted to our vigilance to address their prayers to the Almighty GOD that He might give all His people that peace much desired.


In accordance with pastoral duty we have already ordered that in all Pontifical States public prayers should be addressed to the Clement Father Mercy. But, following the example of predecessors, we moreover resolved to have your prayers joined with those of the whole church. It is therefore, holy brethren, that we ask you by this letter order as soon as possible according to inspirations of your zeal for religion public prayers in your dioceses so that the faithful entrusted to your care after having the help of the powerful intercessions of the very holy and immaculate Virgin Mary Mother of God should pray with ardor and beseech the Almighty whose mercy is inexhaustible, our Lord Jesus Christ to avert from us so great anger, put an end to wars in the whole world, and change the minds of men to fill their hearts with love of Christian peace and by His sovereign virtue that, being all blessed and rooted in faith and charity, applying themselves to practise His holy command, demanding with truly penitent and humble the forgiveness of their sins, avoiding evil and doing good they might follow in all points the path of justice, be penetrated with permanent charity for one another and thus obtain the benefit of peace fertile in fruits of salvation towards God themselves and all men.


We do not doubt at all, venerable brethren, that the feeling which you have for us and the apostolic See will lead you to answer with zeal to the desires and wishes which We have just expressed. But in order that the faithful should pray with more ardor and fruit we will open the treasury of heavenly graces with the dispensation of which the Almighty has entrusted us, and pour their riches upon them.


Therefore grant them in the customary form an indulgence of three hundred days, which they will gain every time that they present prayers and when there shall devoutly pray. Moreover, during the time that those same prayers shall last grant them a plenary indulgence. One won each month the day when purified by the sacrament of penance strengthened by the most holy Eucharist, they shall religiously visit some church and address prayers in the same spirit to God.


It is sweet to us, venerable brethren, to seize upon this occasion to express to you again the feelings of benevolence which we feel for all of you. As a token of esteem, the APOSTOLIC benediction.

rest assured—I am no hypocrite. I
shall never put on a pious exterior to
hide the want of charity in my heart.
As I am, you will always see me."


Mrs. Newton paused again; but as no
one of her visitors showed any inclina-
tion to speak, she continued:


"Only religion is somewhat peculiar,
I believe. I do not keep it as snowy
Sunday but wear it every day. My
essential worship consists in daily dis-
charge of my duty as a wife and moth-
er; my formal worship, in the pious
prostration of my body before my heav-
enly Father, at set times, either in my
closet or in the public assembly. The
Sabbath, to me, is the golden clasp that
binds together the circle of weekly du-
ties. It's a blessing and consolation
just in the degree that the worship of
my six days has been essential wor-
ship."


"And are we to expect nothing from
our minister's wife?" said Miss Lane,
in a very subdued voice. She was evil-
y conscious of having made a great
mistake in her estimate of Mrs. Newton's
character.


"Nothing more than her duties as a
woman. If she have qualities that will
give her a leading social influence,
and have time to spare from her home
duties, which are always first—she
ought to let these qualities become ac-
tive for good. But no more can, with
justice, be required of her than from
any other woman in the congregation.
Your contract for service is with her
husband, and not with her; and you
have no more just claim upon her time,
nor right to control her freedom, than
you have over the wife of your lawyer,
doctor or schoolmaster. It is this mis-
taken idea of people in regard to their
ministers' wives that is producing so
much trouble in societies; and making
wretched the lives of hundreds of poor
women, who hardly dare say that their
souls are their own. It is not enough
that the minister's wife is expected to
keep her house and clothe her children
upon the lowest range of income, that
will not allow her competent help, but
she must spend half of her time in
gossiping around among the idle of
well-to-do ladies of the congregation
who take part in their sewing circles, and at-
tend all their various meetings for good
or doubtful purposes. Now all this is
wrong; and if you are not satisfied
with my husband, because I will not
initiate so bad an example, you must
give him notice accordingly; or if you
think my services absolutely essential
to the prosperity of the church, just
state the amount of salary you can af-
ford to give, and if, for the sum, I can
procure a person in every way as com-
petent as myself to assume the charge
of my children and household, I will
take into serious consideration your
proposition. Beyond this, ladies, I can
promise nothing."


"Thank you again, my dear madam,"
said I, with a warmth that expressed
my real feelings, "for giving this mat-
ter its right solution! You have spoke-
out like a true independent woman, al-
though you are, and I will see that your view-
s are correctly reported. Consider me as
your friend."


She turned upon me a grateful look
and, as she did so, I could see that
my earnest words had brought a dim
moisture to her eyes.


"I would wish," she answered in a
lower voice, "to number you all as my
friends. I have come among you as a
stranger, seeking no pre-eminence, but
only desiring to do my duty as a wo-
man, side by side with other women.
The fact that my husband is your minis-
ter gives me no right to any position above
you, and gives you no right to demand
of me any public service. If my hus-
band fails in his duty, admonish him;
but, in the name of justice and human-
ity, do not establish any supervision
over me. Let my private life be as sa-
cred from intrusion as that of any oth-
er woman. This I have a right to de-
mand, and I will be satisfied with noth-
ing less."


Silenced, if not convinced, was Mis-
s Phebe Lane, and she retired in due time,
with her committee of remonstrance on
accusation, their colors trailing upon.

Detailed information which has been re-
ceived from the seat of war relative to the
slight artillery action near Valenza, in
which the rifled four pounders were first
brought into action, has afforded great sat-
isfaction to military men, and has quieted
many apprehensions, by demonstrating the
practical utility and immense superiority of
the new arm. The telegram is confirmed
that the range was over 500 metres (2734
yards), upwards of mile-and-a-half. The
accuracy of the fire was no less surprising
than the range, and the destructive effect
was still more marvellous. Those who
may have witnessed the experiments at
Vincennes, when the solid masonry forti-
fications were shattered by a few rounds
and yards of stone revetment were tumbled
down, were scarcely prepared for the re-
sults obtained at Valenza against earth-
works. After FIVE rounds, the fortifications
of the Austrians were reduced to
ruins.

It is believed that the effect were due
mainly to the long range, and that at short
distances the fire would have been far less
destructive, as the shot would have made a
clean hole. To understand fully the advan-
tages of the rifled gun, it should be re-
membered that the Napoleon cannon—a
light 12 pounder—cannot be relied upon
for ranges beyond 1000 yards, and that the
infantry rifles will not carry more than 800
yards with accuracy. The French authorities
have represented to an officer of for-
eign army, that they have 200 of these rifled
cannon in Piedmont, and here an artillery
officer said they had 20 batteries or 120
guns. There is good reason, however, to
believe that both statements are exaggera-
ted, and had evidence to-day that the re-
sources of France in modern artillery are
exhausted. This morning the batteries that
were embarked were all smooth bored guns.

graved with the republican motto Liberté,

ization of the French artillery is not sufi-
ciently advanced for a great European

Hamlin was a man of deep piety and unquestionable veracity. He was in the
battle of Thames, and the writer gives
the following as his statement in regard
to the manner in which Tecumseh was
killed:—


He says he was standing but few feet
from Colonel Johnson when he fell, and
in full view, and saw the whole of that
part of the battle. He was well acquainted with Tecumseh, having seen him before the war, and having been prison
or seventeen days, and received many a
cursing from him. He thinks that Tecumseh thought Johnson was Harrison,
as he often heard the chief swear that he
would have Harrison's scalp, and seemed
to have special hatred toward him. —
Johnson's horse fell under him, he himself being also deeply wounded in the
fall he lost his sword, his large pistols
were empty, and he was entangled with
his horse on the ground.


Tecumseh had fired his rifle at him and
when he saw him fall, he threw down
his gun and bounded forward like a tiger
sure of his prey. Johnson had only a
side pistol ready for use. He aimed at
the chief over the head of his horse, and
shot near the centre of his forehead. When the ball struck, it seemed to him
that the Indian jumped with his head full
fifteen feet into the air; and as soon as
he struck the ground, a little Frenchman
ran his bayonet into him, and pinned him
fast to the earth.

"Answer the question," I said. "You had better consult her upon that matter."

"True, my dear child; I admire your delicacy, but run to her on the wings of love. Oh, what a happy man you have made me!"

"I am sure, sir, I am very glad it was in my power to give you pleasure. Do not think you had any reason to doubt my confidence in your wishes."

"There is no reading the human heart, you know—I thought perhaps the difference in our ages—"

"What do two or three years signify?" replied my darling, smiling.

"How odd, indeed, to say that!" I returned, charmed with her delicacy.

"In twenty-five years, only two or three years!"

"But I will go to your mama at once; adieu, darling."

So saying, I hurried from the room, and sent up a message to Mrs. Clarkson, that I wished to see her on important business, and would wait for her in the dining room. In about a quarter of an hour she came downstairs, dressed in most gorgeous manner, but in spite of her toilet, I could not help remarking that she looked thinner and scraggier than ever.

"Mrs. Clarkson," I commenced, making most profound bow, "I wish to talk with you on a very important matter—one which nearly concerns my happiness."

"I shall be pleased to hear what you have to say, sir," replied the widow, taking a seat on the sofa by my side.

"Dear Mrs. Clarkson," I began, for I thought it best to smooth her down, "I have now been an inmate of your house for two months. I need not dwell on the happiness I have enjoyed in your charming society. Your charming daughter and yourself have conspired to make me the happiest of mortals. Your own natural acuteness must have long ago detected that my heart is involved. Yes, my dear madam, I could not gaze on that lovely form without being sensible that this house contained a prize of the most peerless worth. I have even dared to hope—that I may claim that prize as my own, and now only wait your consent."

"Really, sir," stammered the widow, glancing on the carpet, "this confession has taken me unaware; I do not know if my daughter would like—"

"Make your mind easy on that score, my dear Mrs. Clarkson; I have seen your daughter, and have gained her consent to our marriage."

"Thoughtful man!" exclaimed the widow.

I thought this was a strange reply to make, but knew the mother was a little eccentric, and put it down to that score.

"Now, my dear madam," I exclaimed, "I only wait for your answer. Will you consent to make me the happiest man in the United States?"

"Really, sir, this is so unexpected! You take me so much by surprise, I scarcely know what reply to make. I am a poor, lone widow, Mr. Smith. My dear departed husband was a kind husband to me—respect for his memory—"

"My dear madam," interrupted I, "am sure if the late Mr. Clarkson is looking down from heaven this moment, he would give his consent. I am rich, madam; you shall have a house worthy of your kind heart."

"My dear John, I can resist no longer!" and the widow deposited her head of false hair on my heart.

I did not expect this demonstration, and gently removed her head. Nor did at first understand her calling me John—but then, though I was soon to become her son-in-law, she was addressing me finally.

"John!" she exclaimed, "dear John, I will confess the truth, I do love you!"

"You love me?"

"Yes, dear John, your entreaties have prevailed. I consent to be your wife."

And I felt her scraggy arm pass around my neck, and I felt her hard cheek bones.

"Madam!" I exclaimed, "release me! I hear a step."

"No, dear John. I cannot release you. Are you not soon to become my own dear husband?"

And she hugged me again, harder than before.

At that moment the door opened, and the cousin and Miss Clarkson entered the room. When they saw our loving attitude, they retired laughing.

"Madam, there's a mistake!" I exclaimed. "I do not want to marry you, but your daughter!"

"What, sir!" exclaimed the ogress, releasing her hold. "What do you tell me, you bold man? Is this the way you trifle with a lone widow's feelings? You know my daughter is to be married to her cousin next week, and you dare to insult me in this manner—if there's any justice in the land, sir, I'll have it!"

So saying she bounded out of the room.

I received notice to quit that day, and three days afterward an action for breach of promise of marriage was commenced against me. It was in vain my counsel tried to explain the mistake. The evidence was too strong against me, and I was compelled to pay five thousand dollars damages.

Since that day I have become a misanthropist. I hate both men and women, but especially the latter.

FIRE IN ELEVENTH AVENUE—A MAN AND HIS WIFE BADLY BURNED.
At about one o'clock yesterday morning a fire broke out in a shed adjoining the gable end of the frame dwelling house owned by Eben Evans, situated in Eleventh Avenue between Thirty-fifth and Thirty-sixth streets. The flames spread with uncommon swiftness, developing all within their reach. Mr. Evans and wife, and servant girl Mary Dgron, were the only persons in the house. They escaped from the basement without injury, but Mr. and Mrs. Evans, in escaping by the front door, were met by the flames, and having nothing, their night clothes were burned terribly. The hands, arms, back and shoulders of Mrs. Evans were scorched to blister; Mr. Evans was disfigured with his right hand and beard above his head—thus, in his endeavor to save his wife, the top of his head, hand and arm were burned. They fled to the residence of Mr. Burt where they received in attendance of their friends who applied soothing compresses to soothe them. In of burning ruins from Mr. Evans' house the fire extended rapidly to a row of three frame houses, owned by Campbell & Moody, lumber dealers, in use by poor families; they nearly all were destroyed. A Mr. Stable on the rear was also burned to the ground, in which seventeen horses were got out safely. Some were the house of Thirty-sixth street, and prevented the flames from reaching the long block of street, occupied by Campbell & Moody for purposes and tenements for poor families.

Mr. Evans' house was occupied by Mr. Robert Martin. Mr. Evans and wife were merely taking care of Mr. Martin's temporary absence in the country. Mr. Martin's furniture was worth some $1,000 or $1,900, not insured. The house estimated as $5,000, no insurance.

The loss of the other buildings, owned by Campbell & Moody, will probably amount to about $2,500, not insured.

The families burned out as follows:

William Dix—Some portion of his furniture saved; said to be insured.

Mr. Papa, grocer—Some of his stock saved; insurance.

Finnegan Cooney—Very little of his furniture saved.

Patrick O'Brien—Some articles of furniture saved.

Michael Vaughan—Lost most of his furniture.

The aggregate loss will amount to about $4,000.

From all that could be learned appears to be the general impression that the fire was the work of an incendiary.

FIRE IN NEW YORK MEDICAL COLLEGE, EAST THIRTEENTH STREET.
About 8 o'clock yesterday afternoon fire occurred in the roof of the New York Medical College, No. 90 East Thirteenth street. The firemen were promptly on hand and soon extinguished the fire. The building is damaged by fire and water, about $4,000, fully covered by insurance. Fortunately there is no injury done to the students. From appearances, the fire originated from a spark from the chimney connected with a steam engine in the adjoining building.

FIRE AT STUYVESANT'S BAY DESTRUCTION HOTEL—LOSS ABOUT $5,000.
About eleven o'clock yesterday morning fire broke out in the hotel at Strykers Bay occupied by Robert Peboyer. The flames were first discovered in the vicinity of the oven and from thence spread throughout the entire building. Owing to the scarcity of water the flames got beyond the reach of the house, and in a short time the building was consumed and nothing left mark the spot but a pile of ruins. The loss, said, will be about $5,000. Not insured.

BALTIMORE Dec. 16.—The American has received a special dispatch stating that Cook and Coppie attempted escape last night by cutting a hole through the Jail wall. They were fired upon by the sentinels. The prisoners afterwards were heavily ironed.

CHARLESTOWN, Va., Dec. 15.—At half past eight o'clock this evening two of the condemned prisoners escaped from the Jail, and were fired upon by the sentinels and driven back to prison. They are now in the custody of Sheriff Campbell. They had mounted the Jail wall when they were discovered by the sentinel on the outside, who immediately gave alarm and fired upon them. They had sawed their manacles asunder with a barlow knife which they had concealed and made into a fine saw. It is ascertained from their confession that they had been engaged in preparing for their escape during the last ten days. They made a hole in the wall near the window which they had concealed with paper, hiding the bricks they had removed under the bed. Upon the alarm being given they made no resistance, but surrendered as soon as they discovered by the shot of the sentinel that they were detected.

The event has produced the utmost excitement here, and all are on the alert. Major General Taliaferro is directing everything in person, and will maintain an uninterrupted supervision of affairs until after the execution. We do not apprehend any further difficulty.

HARPER'S FERRY, Dec. 15, 2 A.M.—Great excitement prevails here at the present time, on account of the attempted escape of Cook and Coppie. They had cut a hole through the wall and were on the Jail-yard wall, when they were fired upon by the sentinels outside. Another account says that the bars of the window were sawed—but everything is enveloped in mystery. The prisoners are now heavily ironed, and a special guard is standing over them. The streets in front and around the Jail are also kept clear.

SECOND DISPATCH.

The prisoners now say that they got the manacles off their feet by sawing them with an old knife and then forcing the bars.

A misunderstanding occurred several days ago between Gen. Taliaferro and the Jailor, in regard to the placing of sentinels inside of Jail. The Jailor claimed the right to have his own men. The General gave way to him but placed a guard on the outside.

It is discovered that he could have made his escape had he jumped down and strangled the new sentinel.

A Convention of persons opposed to the present Municipal Administration, and also to the Republican Administration of Massachusetts, was held in Faneuil Hall, Boston, on Wednesday last. It was composed of nearly three hundred delegates, representing one hundred and seven towns, and Mr. C. C. Judson presided. The sentiments of this party, which would seem to be American in its utilization, may be learned by the following extracts from the platform adopted by the Convention:

Whereas We are now on the eve of our annual election, which is to determine the character of our State ADMINISTRATION for another year, to be immediately followed by the preparation, excitement, and struggling incident to a Presidential campaign; and whereas we are admonished that the success of either the Republican or the Democratic parties is fraught with great mischief and peril to the country; and that the time now is when we should, if ever, consider and escape, if possible, the danger which Washington, with so much of anxious forethought, has pointed out in his last address to the people of the Republic; and we are determined to do our duty, saved by influence and unbribed by gain; Therefore

Resolved, That the Democratic party is entitled neither to our sympathy nor support, for that, in time of profound political peace, it wantonly threw the brand of discord broadcast over our country, kindling a fire which not only threatened its own destruction, but created confusion and destruction everywhere because it fosters and relies for strength upon influences which are opposed to the intelligence and dangerous to the liberties of any people; and because in its acknowledged and traditional policy it is opposed to the measures calculated to cultivate, develop, and expand the resources and encourage and protect the industry of the country.

Resolved, That We are opposed to the Republican State Administration because it is part and parcel of a party which is opposed to the principles of our Constitution that, by an inherent necessity, it cannot exist as at nearly one-half of the Republic—a party which in one state proclaims itself the peculiar champion of the freedom of a certain race, while in another it denies to the same race the liberty of breathing its air or trading in it; a party which lavishes upon one portion of our citizens professions against hasty naturalization and foreign influence, while in other States, where it has its great strength and controlling power, it crushes out the principle and panders to the worst passions of the foreign element; and, notwithstanding these professions, it here ignores and sets aside, wherever possible, those who would act up to them, and with a contempt hitherto unknown in this Commonwealth, communicates all of its ire to those who dare to disapprove of the acts of its leaders.

Resolved, That there now exists an exigency in the state of public affairs that imperatively calls upon all good citizens to unite at once to putting a stop to these abuses, instituting thorough reforms, and raising this Commonwealth to the grand position which she once held and ought to hold among her sister States.

The Convention nominated the Hon. George W. Briggs for Governor and Increase Sumner for Lt. Governor, and a full ticket of minor State officers.
